# Project Summary {.unnumbered}

Crown-of-thorns starfish (COTS) control depends on finding aggregations before they consume substantial coral. Project CCIP-BR-13 combined fine-scale habitat maps, operational observations, hydrodynamic and connectivity modelling, and a prototype population model to guide searches within reefs and compare control across connected reefs. It addressed the program's Detection & Monitoring and Decisions for Coral Resilience priorities.

The generated habitat maps cover the Great Barrier Reef at 30 m resolution, but provide only weak rankings for subsequent action on their own. Adding recent cull and manta observations improved cull-site selection and surveillance guidance. Retaining approximately the top 80% of sites selected `r p1(oc("sites_selected"))` of candidate sites and retained `r p1(oc("high_retained"))` of observed dives above 0.04 COTS per minute of bottom time. It avoided `r p1(oc("low_avoided"))` of low-density dives (positive CPUE <0.02) and `r p1(oc("ghost_avoided"))` of ghost dives (zero COTS). Dives from 0.02 to 0.04 remained useful culling opportunities and were mostly retained. Candidate-site coverage and recorded dive effort differed; annual checks must address initially missed high-density dives.

The same rule could avoid `r p1(oc("manta_distance_avoided"))` of recorded straight-line tow distance. This estimate retains nearby tows outside site polygons; further reductions may be possible but remain untested. The delivered layers also identify high-ranked habitat outside regular search areas for exploration. Habitat-only tow selection did not outperform evenly spaced thinning.

Products include a 2027 ranking of `r int(n_sites)` cull sites and reproducible workflows. Lizard Island larval-concentration maps illustrate a basis for interpreting future fine-scale connectivity data. The COTS–coral model, integrated with AIMS's ADRIA framework, reproduces historical irruption patterns, represents the emerging fifth wave and supports exploratory scenarios through 2050. Density mismatches, independent validation and the complete assessment of control since 2012 remain outstanding.

Regular GBRMPA meetings guided delivery and in-water testing plans. April and June 2026 Malu engagement supported a separate future Far Northern model. A delivery workshop is planned for 5 November 2026, followed by January–February 2027 vessel trials. Realised detection, effort and coral-protection benefits require measurement.

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Context & Objectives

## The management problem

Irruptions of crown-of-thorns starfish (*Acanthaster* cf. *solaris*; COTS) are a major cause of coral loss on the Great Barrier Reef [@death2012decline; @pratchett2017thirty]. The COTS Control Program suppresses irruptions by manual culling, which can protect coral when sustained at the right reefs [@matthews2024protecting]. A substantial portion of operational effort goes into searching for COTS, creating opportunities to improve where surveillance and culling are directed.

Manta tow surveillance records COTS and feeding scars and assesses reef irruption status. Crews then choose cull sites using manta results and previous culling records. The current EoTR register contains `r int(n_sites)` designated sites on `r int(n_reefs)` reefs, of which approximately 1,300 sites across 200 actioned reefs are typically culled each year [@gbrmpadashboard2026]. The dashboards bring together recent observations to support these decisions [@matthews2025intelligence]. In the held-out cull records from 2018 to 2026, `r p0(cs_ghost / cs_dives)` of dives found no COTS (ghost dives), and a further `r p0(cs_low / cs_dives)` found COTS at CPUE below 0.02 COTS per minute of bottom time (low-density dives).
<!-- Approximate annual site/reef activity supplied by the author in review 02,
with the COTS Dashboard as source. Confirm reporting period for the approximate
1,300-site figure before finalisation; register totals remain inline results. -->

The operational strategy links decisions from individual sites to voyages and regional priorities [@fletcher2020strategy]. In practice, tow routes mostly follow established cull sites around reef perimeters. Many sites were initially delineated from satellite maps in 2018, leaving gaps in lagoon bommie fields, shallow crests and isolated patches. Search can therefore repeatedly trigger dives where few COTS are found while overlooking other potential habitat. Reducing repeated searches in low-priority areas could free effort to search these gaps, improving both efficiency and the chance of finding previously undetected populations.
<!-- Current practice and the history of site delineation supplied by the author
in review 02; Fletcher supports the operational framework, not these specific
observations about the current site register. -->

Crews and GBRMPA analysts already hold useful information about recent culling, empty sites, and COTS or scars seen on manta tows. This knowledge is strongest on frequently visited reefs and within the established search footprint. Fine-scale habitat maps cover places with little recent evidence, including potential search areas outside that footprint, but say little about whether COTS are present this season. This project combines these sources to prioritise familiar sites and identify additional places to search.

## Earlier models this project builds on

Most COTS modelling has treated whole reefs as its spatial units, either across the GBR for regional planning [@condie2021interventions; @bozec2022cumulative; @matthews2020cotsmod] or on individual reefs to inform culling thresholds [@morello2014model; @plaganyi2020targets]. Reef-level species distribution models (SDMs), which relate species observations to environmental conditions, showed that larval connectivity and water quality explain much of the spatial distribution of irruptions [@matthews2020connectivity], and a hybrid machine-learning model estimates each reef's annual irruption probability [@stewart2026hybrid]. Population and ecosystem models help compare regional control strategies and ecological targets, but their whole-reef units do not identify where within a reef to search or cull.

Recent developments support finer spatial resolution. Coral species distribution models use satellite-derived multiscale terrain and benthic variables to map habitat for key coral taxa at tens of metres [@guillaume2025coral]. Their predictions and environmental predictors are inputs to the habitat modelling here, which maps COTS suitability at 30 m and combines it with recent program observations.

In parallel, advances in hydrodynamic and COTS larval-connectivity modelling provide a route to representing connections among smaller areas of reef. This project adapts COTSMod, a spatially explicit model of COTS populations and coral recovery [@matthews2020cotsmod], to represent site-level dynamics in the northern GBR irruption initiation box. It uses AIMS's high-throughput ADRIA ecosystem modelling framework and CoralBlox coral dynamics [@adriamethods2026; @dealmeida2026coralblox]. The prototype covers the Lizard Island cluster, with 2,895 sub-reef sites on 113 reefs. Its present transport inputs remain at reef scale; the fine-scale hydrodynamic network has not yet replaced them. This distinction matters when interpreting its capacity to represent within-reef differences ([the population-model Methods](#sec-metacommunity)).

## The decisions this work supports

The tactical work addresses two operational uses: reducing manta tow effort while retaining detection of COTS aggregations, and searching fewer cull sites while avoiding empty or low-density dives. For management, the priority is to retain dives above 0.04 COTS per minute of bottom time. Missing some dives between 0.02 and 0.04 is acceptable under the proposed operational decision criterion; these should not carry the same penalty as missed dives above 0.04. The 0.04 value is the management target used here, while ecological sustainability also depends on coral cover [@plaganyi2020targets; @gbrmpadashboard2026]. The existing retrospective analyses used ≥0.02 to define a problematic dive and <0.02 for a low-density dive. Those results are retained under their original definitions, alongside a separate evaluation of the unchanged rankings against the >0.04 management criterion ([the cull-site Results](#sec-high-density)).

Reducing search effort can miss COTS even when sites are dropped without a model. The evaluation therefore asks whether a ranking finds more aggregations or retains more high-density dives than random selection at the same effort. For manta surveillance, it also compares model selection with evenly spaced tows. These comparisons distinguish the value of the ranking from the saving achieved simply by searching less. Additional searches outside the familiar footprint address a separate question: whether effort released from repeat searches can improve coverage and detection elsewhere.

A strategic decision sits above these: how to allocate control among connected reefs in a cluster or region. When should culling stop on a heavily affected reef if its remaining coral cannot be protected? When should control continue on a reef whose COTS population cannot be brought below a local target, because reducing its larval export could protect other reefs? A site-level model of population growth, collapse, dispersal and coral consumption is needed to compare those consequences. Evidence of renewed population growth at Lizard Island [@chandler2023densities; @uthicke2024edna] also motivates assessing whether the emerging fifth primary irruption wave can be suppressed, and what resources this would require.

## Project priorities and objectives

The Work Plan identifies Decisions for Coral Resilience and Detection & Monitoring as the priority research areas. The bridging project adapts coral-habitat and hydrodynamic capabilities developed through linked NESP and RRAP work to COTS decisions, rather than duplicating those investments. The completed habitat and search evaluations address tactical planning; the Lizard Island prototype establishes the basis for strategic tests. Appendix E maps the Work Plan outputs to the evidence and remaining development needs.

The specific project objectives were to:

- Develop GBR-wide predictive fine-scale habitat suitability models by connecting fine-scale COTS data to new high-resolution benthic and coral habitat data.
- Optimise and standardise surveillance paths to improve irruption detection and operational efficiency, including a comparison against traditional perimeter-based surveillance.
- Refine site-level management strategies for individual reefs through predicted suitable habitat and metapopulation modelling.

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Methods

## Observations and habitat information

The analyses used existing Control Program and monitoring records across the GBR. Cull records covered 2002–2026; after excluding missing catches and invalid bottom time, matched records represented `r int(crscope$matched_sites)` designated sites on `r int(crscope$matched_reefs)` reefs. Catch per unit effort (CPUE) was COTS culled per minute of bottom time. Habitat fitting used site-year summaries; operational assessment used individual dive outcomes.



The archived habitat response was CPUE ≥0.02. Ghost dives found no COTS; low-density dives had positive CPUE <0.02. The separate management assessment retained dives strictly above 0.04, the program's ecological target where coral cover is below 40% [@plaganyi2020targets; @gbrmpadashboard2026]. Dives from 0.02 to 0.04 inclusive remained a separate intermediate group of useful culling opportunities. Existing rankings were reassessed, without refitting to the higher threshold.

Manta tows supplied COTS sightings and feeding-scar observations. Strong evidence meant a direct sighting, at least two counted scars, or scars recorded as common in legacy surveys. Records with neither COTS nor scars were negatives. Scooter-assisted large area diver-based surveys and Reef Health and Impact Surveys contributed to the explanatory habitat model [@pratchett2022salad; @beeden2014rhis]. ReefScan sightings supplied a separate presence-only check; missing effort tracks prevented a detection-rate estimate [@bainbridge2024reefscan].

Habitat predictors described depth, seabed shape, exposure, turbidity and predicted habitat for three *Acropora* taxa, assembled at 30 m resolution [@guillaume2025coral; @reefguide2026; @gbrmpabathymetry2021; @gbrmpageomorphic2021; @roelfsema2021shallow]. The search map used the model with extra environmental predictors where available and the full-extent model elsewhere. Appendix B lists predictors; Appendix G gives model definitions and data-access checks. No new sampling of COTS or coral was undertaken for these model fits. ## Testing habitat and recent-evidence rankings

Habitat models ranked locations within reefs. The operational ranking combined a site's habitat with the preceding season's cull and nearby manta evidence through a logistic regression. Its score was:

$$
\begin{aligned}
s_i &= \beta_0+\beta_H H_i+\beta_P P_i+\beta_Q Q_i+\beta_R R_i\\
&\quad+\beta_E\log(1+E_i)+\beta_M\log(1+M_i)+\beta_T\log(1+T_i).
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $H_i$ is the mean habitat score inside site $i$, ranked among designated sites on its reef. $P_i$ records whether any recent dive there reached CPUE ≥0.02; $Q_i$ records a searched site where none did. $R_i$ is the distance-weighted proportion of nearby dives reaching ≥0.02; $E_i$ is the weighted count of dives. $M_i$ and $T_i$ are weighted counts of strong-evidence and all nearby manta tows. Nearby records receive decreasing weights out to 900 m. Coefficients ($\beta$) were estimated jointly from dive outcomes at ≥0.02, rather than assigned as rules. All sites were ordered by decreasing score on each reef. Appendix G gives the distance equation, coefficients, missing-data treatment and priority classes.

The score incorporates crew behaviour as well as habitat. Evaluation used habitat fits that withheld the reef's group. For 2019–2026, the evidence regression used only earlier seasons; the habitat component was spatially held out but was not also restricted to earlier years.

Comparisons kept candidate-site coverage or high-density-dive retention equal. All designated sites were candidates, including never-dived sites; outcomes at unvisited sites remained unknown. Random selection provided exact expectations at the same site count. Repeated visits meant equal site counts did not imply equal numbers of recorded dives or equal time. Class-specific retention or avoidance used all dives in that CPUE class as its denominator; deferred-dive composition instead used all deferred dives. Manta surveys were also compared with evenly spaced thinning of linked strong-evidence tows. Tow order was approximated from position, so thinning assessed existing surveys rather than new routes.

We evaluated 80%, 90%, 95% and 99% high-density retention and the product's A–C rule, which selects sites with descending rank divided by reef site count ≤0.8. Separate spatial estimates counted whole tow segments and straight-line distance lying only within deferred sites. Surveillance outside designated polygons or overlapping retained sites remained. These estimates assumed retained cull visits still occurred. Uncertainty resampled whole reef-years; Appendix G documents interpolation, integer rounding, geometry exclusions and the 500 paired bootstrap draws.

## Seasonal search products

The 2027 ranking used the latest available 12 months, June 2025–May 2026, and assigned sites to classes A–D. Exploration areas marked high-ranked habitat outside designated sites and recent tow paths (@fig-2027). Annual or pre-closure checks of deferred sites, triggered revisits and exploration must be counted when testing annual effort and detection.

## Water movement and larval connections {#sec-hydro-connectivity-methods}

The dispersal assessment compared daily mean larval concentrations at ages 5, 9 and 10 days for `r int(lc_scope$releases)` releases during December 2022–January 2023. Values were averaged by area to sub-reef sites and reefs, then ranked within releases. Hotspot persistence and cross-shelf patterns described relative exposure, without identifying origins, settlement or source-to-destination connectivity. Appendix K gives the comparisons.

## Connected COTS and coral populations {#sec-metacommunity}

The Lizard Island prototype represents `r int(lc_scope$sites)` sites on `r int(lc_scope$reefs)` reefs. COTSMod supplies population stages, predation and larval processes; ADRIA handles the spatial domain and disturbances, coupled to CoralBlox coral dynamics [@matthews2020cotsmod; @cotsmodmethods2026; @adriamethods2026; @dealmeida2026coralblox]. Transport remains reef-to-reef; fine-scale hydrodynamic connections have not replaced it.

Calibration compared irruption timing, size, troughs and coral change on four monitoring reefs. Recorded culling was applied as removals limited by available animals. Paired scenarios used matching environmental forcing and random seeds. Initial projections linked diver-hours to removals through a density-dependent catch rate and compared control effort under two climate pathways through 2050. Appendix I describes the current calibration and projections; Appendix G retains equations, assumptions and the planned assessment of culling since 2012.

## Engagement with Rights-holders and Management Stakeholders {#sec-engagement}

GBRMPA meetings throughout the project guided delivery, including the decision to rank designated cull sites. Earlier informal feedback also informed map formats, uncertainty communication and integration with existing planning systems. The progress report records November discussions with Malu Ventures and Jabalbina about interpretation and operator use.

Engagement with Malu included an April 2026 visit and June follow-up. Fine-scale observations were collected for a standalone Far Northern species distribution model planned for future development; they were not used to fit the models assessed here. A final delivery workshop is planned for 5 November 2026. Trials of habitat plus recent-evidence rankings are planned aboard BPM in Cairns and with Malu in the Far Northern GBR and Torres Strait during January–February 2027. These trials will compare the recommendations with crew practice and record detection, effort and follow-up at deferred sites.

# Results

## GBR fine-scale habitat predictions {#sec-cull}

### Habitat layers: a consistent first ordering on every reef {.unnumbered}

The habitat layers provide a first search order across the GBR, including reefs with little recent evidence. Their absolute values vary with survey year and region (@fig-overview); within reefs, the cull-trained layers place their highest ranks along reef margins and outer slopes (@fig-maps).

![Within-reef habitat ranks on Eyrie, Batt, Broadhurst and Lady Musgrave reefs. Columns show the full-extent and limited-extent cull-trained models, the manta-trained model, the joint habitat model, habitat updated with cull history for 2027, and joint-model uncertainty (90% posterior interval width). The top 30% of each reef is emphasised. Satellite imagery: Esri World Imagery; full attribution is in Appendix H.](../outputs/figures/fig02b_four_reef_comparison_imagery.png){#fig-maps width="100%"}

On their own, the layers discriminate modestly between places on the same reef. On independent manta tows, the limited-extent habitat model reached a within reef-year AUC of `r ci3(mi("RG + year", "within_reef_year_auc"), mi("RG + year", "auc_low"), mi("RG + year", "auc_high"))` (@tbl-manta, @fig-manta). It placed `r p0(mi("RG + year", "top20_lift") - 1)` more strong-evidence tows in each reef's top-ranked 20% than chance. The manta model, trained on tows but scored leave-reef-out, reached `r ci3(mt("within", "auc"), mt("within", "auc", "low"), mt("within", "auc", "high"))` (Appendix H).

### Predicted habitat and recent evidence increase cull-site search efficiency {#sec-high-density}

Combining recent cull and manta observations with habitat improved cull-site selection compared with habitat alone. This pattern held across seasons (Appendix H). The assessment compared sites selected for cull dives and the share of observed high-density dives (>0.04 CPUE) they retained. In the test over 2019–2026 (`r int(fw_dives)` dives in `r int(fw_ry)` reef-years), retaining 80% of those dives required selecting `r hdci("sites_searched", 0.8)` of designated sites with habitat estimates plus recent observations; retaining 90% required `r hdci("sites_searched", 0.9)`. Both required fewer sites than habitat alone or random selection at the same retention (Appendix H, @tbl-search-highlights).

At the proposed A–C cutoff, avoiding the bottom approximately 20% of sites removed `r occi("low_avoided")` of low-density cull dives (positive CPUE <0.02) and `r occi("ghost_avoided")` of ghost cull dives (zero COTS). It retained `r odci("intermediate_retained")` of dives from 0.02 to 0.04 inclusive. Retaining this intermediate group is useful: those dives remain suitable culling opportunities even though the assessment gives highest priority to retaining dives above 0.04.

Search reductions became smaller as retention increased. Retaining 95% required `r hdci("sites_searched")` of sites with the combined ranking, avoiding `r p1(hd("low_avoided"))` of low-density dives and `r p1(hd("ghost_avoided"))` of ghost dives. Retaining 99% required `r hdci("sites_searched", 0.99)` of sites and avoided only `r p1(hd("low_avoided", 0.99))` and `r p1(hd("ghost_avoided", 0.99))` of those dive classes, respectively.

Deferring class D, the bottom-20% rule shown in @fig-2027, selected `r occi("sites_selected")` of cull sites and retained `r occi("high_retained")` of observed >0.04 dives. It initially omitted `r p1(1 - oc("high_retained"))` of those dives. This is close to the 90% retention option. Random selection of the same number of sites retained `r occi("high_retained", "random")` of high-density dives. Annual or pre-closure checks could recover missed populations, but their success and additional effort were not evaluated ([the operational impact pathway](#sec-monitoring)).

Equal candidate-site counts did not represent equal dive effort. The ranking deferred `r odci("all_dives_avoided")` of recorded dives, compared with `r odci("all_dives_avoided", "random")` under random site selection, because it retained more repeatedly visited sites. Of its `r int(sum(opbreakdown$deferred_dives))` deferred dives, `r p1(od("quiet_share_deferred"))` were ghost or low-density, compared with `r p1(od("quiet_share_deferred", "random"))` under random selection. @tbl-operational-highlights gives all four classes. These composition percentages use deferred dives as their denominator, unlike the class-specific retention and avoidance percentages above. The comparison shows better protection of useful culling opportunities at equal candidate-site coverage; it does not compare equal dive counts or measured search time.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-operational-highlights
#| tbl-cap: "Retaining classes A–C and deferring D, 2019–2026. Percentages [95% reef-year bootstrap intervals]. Both rankings select the same candidate-site count, not the same recorded dive count. Upper rows use all sites, all dives or all dives in the stated CPUE class as their denominator. Lower rows describe the composition of deferred dives and sum to 100% in each column. Tow reductions are conditional spatial estimates before annual checks and exploration, assuming retained cull visits still occur. Full matched-retention comparisons are in Appendix H."
op_metrics <- c("sites_selected","all_dives_avoided","high_retained","intermediate_retained","low_avoided","ghost_avoided","manta_tows_avoided","manta_distance_avoided",
 "share_deferred_ghost","share_deferred_low","share_deferred_intermediate","share_deferred_high")
op_labels <- c("Candidate cull sites selected","All recorded dives avoided","Dives above 0.04 CPUE retained","Dives at 0.02–0.04 CPUE retained","Low-density dives avoided (0 < CPUE <0.02)","Ghost dives avoided (CPUE = 0)","Whole manta tows potentially avoided","Manta distance potentially avoided",
 "Ghost: CPUE = 0","Low: 0 < CPUE <0.02","Intermediate: 0.02 ≤ CPUE ≤0.04","High: CPUE >0.04")
op_value <- function(m,score,col) if(m %in% opcut$metric) oc(m,score,col) else od(m,score,col)
op_format <- function(score) vapply(op_metrics, function(m) sprintf("%.1f [%.1f–%.1f]",100*op_value(m,score,"value"),100*op_value(m,score,"low"),100*op_value(m,score,"high")),"")
op_rows <- data.frame(Outcome=op_labels,`Habitat + recent observations`=op_format("combined"),`Random selection`=op_format("random"),check.names=FALSE)
op_rows <- rbind(op_rows[1:8,],setNames(data.frame("**Composition of deferred dives**","",""),names(op_rows)),op_rows[9:12,])
knitr::kable(op_rows,row.names=FALSE)
```


Habitat alone separated locations with and without COTS only weakly. Its practical contribution was to cover places where recent observations were absent: `r p0(n_noev / nrow(pri))` of designated sites in the 2027 product were on reefs without dives or tows in the preceding 12 months. Those sites relied on habitat and should be treated as initial search priorities. Past observations carried most of the information on recently visited reefs, but also reflected where crews chose to work. Maps, habitat comparisons and tests beyond the familiar footprint are in Appendix H.

Manta surveillance required a separate effort estimate (@tbl-operational-highlights; Appendix H). At the A–C cutoff, `r occi("manta_tows_avoided")` of recorded tows lay entirely within deferred-only sites, and `r occi("manta_distance_avoided")` of recorded straight-line tow distance lay within those sites. The distance estimate allows shortening a tow; the tow-count estimate omits only whole segments. Both keep surveillance outside designated sites and in any overlap with retained sites. The >0.04 retention values describe cull dives at selected sites, conditional on those dives still occurring. They do not establish detection after removing the corresponding manta surveillance, or annual savings after follow-up and exploration.

In the retrospective manta comparison, habitat-only selection did not outperform evenly spaced thinning. That comparison is an analytical benchmark; practical searches require crew judgement and recent observations alongside habitat. Appendix H retains the surveillance comparisons.

### Seasonal products and exploration {.unnumbered}

The delivered ranking covers `r int(n_sites)` designated sites on `r int(n_reefs)` reefs. Its map shows search priority and the recent evidence behind each site.

The product also identifies `r int(nrow(expl))` exploration areas on `r int(length(unique(expl$reef_name)))` reefs, outside designated sites and recent tow paths (@fig-2027). These allow operators to direct some effort toward overlooked habitat. Historical observations on new ground supported investigating such gaps, but the proposed exploration areas themselves have not been trialled. Their detection yield and the annual effort required for added searches and deferred-site checks remain to be estimated or measured.

## Preliminary larval dispersal patterns vary across the reef cluster {#sec-hydro-connectivity-results}

The larval-concentration maps showed uneven exposure to simulated larvae across `r int(lc_scope$sites)` sub-reef sites on `r int(lc_scope$reefs)` reefs during the 2022–23 spawning season. Persistent day-10 hotspots were concentrated on mid-shelf reefs south of the Lizard Island group, including Williamson, Mackay and Osterlund (@fig-larval-hotspots). Reefs toward the northern end of the domain generally ranked lower.

![Persistence of simulated larval-concentration hotspots at day 10, across the model domain (A) and around Lizard Island (B). Colour shows the proportion of releases in which a sub-reef site ranked in the highest fifth of concentration within that release. The dashed box marks the enlarged area; grey shows land. This reformats concentration figure lc2 from the project analysis. High concentration does not by itself establish local retention, source strength or settlement.](../outputs/figures/fig28_larval_hotspot_persistence.png){#fig-larval-hotspots width="100%"}

The Lizard Island group was not a persistent concentration hotspot at the later larval ages examined. Some releases produced higher concentrations around Lizard earlier in development, but these peaks generally did not persist (Appendix K). This may partly reflect the domain boundary, which excludes larval sources on reefs outside the model.

Cross-shelf patterns differed along the domain. In its central part, later-age concentrations were generally higher on mid-shelf reefs than on Ribbon Reefs at similar latitudes; the southern Ribbon Reefs did not show the same deficit. The mid-shelf–Ribbon contrast qualitatively matches the irruption contrasts in the regional monitoring checks (Appendix I), while the one-season concentration result remains sensitive to the domain boundary.

Following this project, network analysis will examine when reefs in the initiation box exchange larvae within tightly connected groups, and when groups become relatively isolated. Combining these results with larval-concentration patterns could identify periods and locations favourable to irruption initiation or escalation and feed into an early-warning system. The planned work will compare these signals with long-term monitoring and reef-level irruption estimates [@stewart2026hybrid]. Appendix K describes the network tests needed to assess this use.

## Historical COTS and coral dynamics provide a basis for testing control strategies {#sec-metacommunity-results}

The updated metacommunity model reproduced the broad sequence of historical irruption waves and coral decline and recovery on the four calibration reefs (@fig-metacommunity-cots-coral). The comparison used `r int(mcn("base_seeds"))` random-seed pairs, with additional parameter tests giving `r int(mcn("calibration_arms_per_cull_state"))` runs each with and without recorded culling. Lizard Island's first (1990s) COTS peak remains too small, and coral trajectories differed from the surveys in some periods. Manta and photo-transect coral estimates also differed because they sampled different parts of the reef. Initial effort scenarios through 2050 reduced simulated near-term COTS peaks, but coral gains varied among reefs and climate pathways; these exploratory comparisons demonstrate capability rather than likely outcomes (Appendix I).

![Historical COTS and coral dynamics on the calibration reefs, combining source Figures 1 and 4 from the 21 October snapshot. Left: manta-tow equivalents (dotted line: 0.22 COTS per tow). Right: hard coral cover, modelled relative to habitable area. Blue solid lines omit recorded culling; purple dashed lines apply it. Lines are five-seed means; darker bands span those seeds and lighter bands span all 65 parameter-test runs per culling state. These ranges are not confidence intervals. Black points show LTMP manta observations (coral bars: reported 95% intervals); orange diamonds show 9 m photo-transects. Survey supports differ. These are calibration and diagnostic comparisons.](../outputs/figures/fig22_metacommunity_cots_coral.png){#fig-metacommunity-cots-coral width="100%"}

The model represents the build-up of the fifth primary irruption wave, but exceeds observed densities on several reefs. This overshoot could understate the relative effect of contemporary culling, a sensitivity that requires testing. The paired culling trajectories demonstrate the model's response to recorded removals; they do not yet provide an independently validated estimate of the program's impact since 2012.



{{< pagebreak >}}

# Discussion & Outputs

## Combining recent observations with habitat

The main tactical finding is that recent observations improve the order in which designated cull sites are searched, while habitat supplies an initial ordering where observations are absent. This extends the program's existing use of surveillance and crew knowledge [@fletcher2020strategy; @matthews2025intelligence]. The maps make that information more consistent and available across vessels. Their value lies in the comparison with random or simpler selection at the same effort, rather than in the reduction obtained simply by omitting sites.

Habitat alone ranked locations on the same reef weakly. This is compatible with reef-level distribution studies showing the importance of connectivity and conditions associated with irruption development [@matthews2020connectivity; @stewart2026hybrid]. Static terrain and coral habitat cannot describe the current stage of an irruption, recent removals or movement of aggregations. The recent-evidence ranking captures some of those changes, but also captures where crews chose to work. It should be interpreted as operational knowledge combined with habitat, rather than independent confirmation that a preferred location holds COTS.

The distinction matters most on rarely visited reefs and beyond designated sites. Prioritising repeated finds can continually direct effort towards the same footprint. Exploration areas provide a way to examine suitable habitat outside it, including lagoon patches and other places poorly covered by perimeter surveillance. Those areas remain hypotheses about useful search locations. Records from new ground support investigating such gaps, but do not establish the detection yield of the proposed areas. Recording nil observations and effort will be as important as recording finds.

## Retention, surveillance and the cost of deferral

The A–C rule offers a concrete entry point for operational testing. It retains approximately nine in ten observed high-density dives while selecting approximately four in five candidate cull sites. Most dives from 0.02 to 0.04 are also retained, preserving useful culling opportunities below the ecological target. Ghost and low-density dives form a larger share of the deferred set than under random site selection. Nevertheless, the extra avoidance of those dive classes is small, and the ranking keeps more recorded dives overall than random selection of the same site count. The comparison supports protection of useful dives at equal candidate-site coverage; a matched-dive-effort comparison is needed to isolate gains in dive efficiency. Remaining high-density omissions require agreed tolerances and follow-up. The relevant target also depends on coral cover and the purpose of control [@plaganyi2020targets; @matthews2024protecting].

The separate manta estimate improves the interpretation of effort. Fewer cull sites selected does not translate directly into the same percentage fewer tows, because recorded segments cross site boundaries and include surveillance elsewhere. The geometry calculation preserves portions needed by retained sites and all portions outside designated sites, including nearby tows that do not intersect them. This conservatively limits the spatial accounting; further reductions outside polygons may be possible, but their feasibility and detection consequences are untested. The estimate does not show that crews would make the same dive decisions after associated manta evidence was removed, nor whether a shortened route saves vessel time.

The retrospective tow comparison reinforces the need for coverage. Habitat-only selection did not outperform evenly spaced thinning, although the latter is an analytical benchmark based on recorded surveys. Practical route planning must account for workability, travel, crew judgement and recent observations. A poor result for habitat-only thinning does not remove habitat's role in identifying additional places to search; it does rule out claiming that the habitat score alone supplies an improved exclusion rule.

Annual full surveys, pre-closure checks and revisits triggered by new evidence could detect populations initially deferred. They cannot guarantee that a missed aggregation will be found before coral is consumed. Later detections may also represent new population growth rather than an original false negative. An initial audit of deferred sites, together with dated follow-up and a maximum acceptable delay, is needed to distinguish these outcomes. Full-season effort must include those checks, repeat dives and exploration. January–February 2027 trials should test the ranking against normal crew planning before an annual saving is claimed.

## Using connected population models for strategic decisions

The metacommunity strand addresses a different management scale: how culling on one reef affects COTS and coral there and on connected reefs. Reef-scale ecosystem models have already established the importance of comparing control strategies under interacting disturbances [@morello2014model; @condie2021interventions; @bozec2022cumulative]. This prototype builds on COTSMod within a framework that can connect site-level habitat, population processes and intervention scenarios [@matthews2020cotsmod; @adriamethods2026]. Keeping the COTS equations in a reusable package also allows their use in other modelling frameworks.

The historical comparisons provide evidence that the framework can reproduce broad irruption cycles and respond to recorded removals. They remain calibration and diagnostics. Peak sizes, densities between waves and the recent build-up depend on coral assumptions and the relationship between manta observations and true abundance. Recent cull and diver observations also informed the corrected larval inputs, so agreement with those observations is not independent validation. The excess simulated COTS carried into the near-term projections could affect the apparent benefit of culling. That sensitivity needs testing before estimates of coral protected are used in decisions.

The intended assessment of control since 2012 must compare paired histories beginning from the same population and coral state. Holding outside larval supply constant estimates the effect of control inside the model domain under unchanged outside conditions. A regional no-control history instead needs outside supply consistent with no control on those reefs. Those are different questions, and the existing reef-level irruption predictions do not supply the second counterfactual by themselves. Requested catches that exceed simulated availability must also remain visible, rather than being treated as successful removals.

For the fifth primary irruption wave, the useful comparison is among feasible allocations of present capacity, additional effort and rules for beginning or stopping control. A reef with little coral left to protect may still supply larvae to neighbours. Conversely, fewer COTS need not yield lasting local coral gains if heat stress or cyclones remove the spared coral. Scenarios must therefore follow larval export, downstream populations and coral recovery as well as local catches. The initial projections demonstrate this capability; they do not yet identify a preferred management strategy.

Larval-concentration hotspots provide a complementary regional signal, but concentration is not equivalent to settlement, local retention or source strength. Release-specific networks, distance-based comparisons and explicit tests of the northern boundary are needed before a hydrodynamic early-warning interpretation is supported. The metacommunity model still uses reef-level transport. Coupling the new habitat layers or fine-scale connections to intervention decisions is a subsequent test, rather than a completed integration. Appendix L retains the scenario and field-assessment design.

## Final project outputs

The outputs and their current evidence status are:

- GBR-wide 30 m habitat-suitability and search-priority layers, with a separate layer showing known aggregation locations and accompanying uncertainty products.
- The 2027 designated cull-site ranking and exploration-area products in CSV and KMZ formats, supported by spatial and season-by-season evaluation.
- Retrospective surveillance and cull-site comparisons, including the >0.04 retention assessment and separate conditional tow-effort estimates; operational deployment remains to be trialled.
- Lizard Island larval-concentration products and a reproducible COTS–coral metacommunity prototype with calibration diagnostics and initial control scenarios; fine-scale network delivery and independent validation remain open.
- This technical report and documented analysis workflows. Public repository registration, release identifiers and the final rights-holder information package require completion (Appendices E and F).

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Outcomes & Impact Pathway

## More efficient control through operational testing

The Work Plan selects CCIP Outcome 2, a more effective, efficient and scalable response to COTS irruptions, and Outcome 4, decisions informed by biophysical and predictive knowledge. The project contributes through explicit search priorities, measurable trade-offs and a platform for strategic comparisons. The outputs establish capability; reduced annual costs, improved detection and additional coral protection are intended outcomes that have not yet been demonstrated.

For Outcome 2, the immediate users are Control Program managers, vessel planners and dive teams. The ranking converts habitat and recent observations into a common site order that can be refreshed each season. This supports testing whether repeat searches at lower-priority sites can be deferred and whether some effort can be redirected to overlooked habitat. The 10–15% proposed reductions in surveillance searches and low-density or empty dives remain adoption targets. They require an agreed allowance for missed >0.04 dives, reliable follow-up coverage and a complete account of effort.

Repeated GBRMPA meetings shaped delivery, including the choice to rank designated cull sites. This aligns the product with locations crews already recognise and record, while the exploration component addresses the limits of that register. The planned 5 November 2026 workshop will support final interpretation and agreement on delivery and integration. Product files can support Field Maps and COTS Dashboard workflows, but the report does not claim that either integration or routine uptake is complete.

## Co-interpretation with rights-holders and operators

The engagement described in Methods provides a direct pathway to testing usefulness with Traditional Owner operators. Malu's April visit and June follow-up also collected fine-scale observations for a future standalone Far Northern model. Those observations are an additional resource for subsequent work, rather than evidence validating the current GBR-wide ranking. Clear separation of the two avoids overstating where the delivered models have been tested.

January–February 2027 trials are planned aboard BPM in Cairns and with Malu in the Far Northern GBR and Torres Strait. They will compare habitat plus recent evidence with normal planning, record departures from the recommended order and assess how crews interpret low ranks. Independent checks of deferred sites will help estimate initial false negatives; annual and pre-closure checks will assess later detection and delay. All follow-up and exploration effort must enter the seasonal comparison. Agreement on monitoring ownership, reporting and the acceptable omission rate is needed before trial findings can support adoption.

## Predictive knowledge for cluster-scale management

For Outcome 4, the population model and dispersal analyses provide a framework for comparing control across connected reefs, including cases where local and downstream benefits differ. The intended users include GBRMPA planners and researchers developing control scenarios. The next steps are to resolve the recent population mismatch, complete independent checks and agree feasible effort and external-supply assumptions before estimating program impact since 2012 or recommending fifth-wave suppression strategies.

The delivery pathway therefore links documented consultation to field testing, repeatable evaluation and only then wider use. Suitable metadata, accessible product versions and clear limits are necessary for other researchers and managers to reproduce the comparisons. Data access and outstanding release requirements are stated below. No benefit is attributed to a model merely because it produces a map or a scenario trajectory.

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Conclusions & Next Steps

This bridging project established a repeatable way to combine fine-scale habitat with recent operational evidence, rank every designated cull site and identify habitat beyond the usual search footprint. Recent observations supplied most of the tactical gain. Habitat alone discriminated weakly within reefs but provided coverage where current evidence was absent.

The proposed A–C cutoff makes the management choice explicit: it selected `r p1(oc("sites_selected"))` of candidate sites and retained `r p1(oc("high_retained"))` of observed >0.04 dives. Conditional spatial estimates suggest reductions in whole manta tows and distance, but the initially missed high-density dives and the effort of annual checks prevent treating these as established annual savings. The next operational step is the planned January–February 2027 vessel trial, with an agreed omission allowance, checks of deferred sites and comparison against normal crew practice.

At cluster scale, the COTS–coral prototype and larval-concentration products extend the capacity to ask where control could protect local and downstream coral. Independent validation, the recent population-state mismatch, boundary supply and feasible effort must be resolved before historical program-impact estimates or fifth-wave strategies can guide management. Fine-scale hydrodynamic connections and habitat-informed control remain candidate extensions.

The most significant change is the availability of explicit, reproducible decisions and comparisons at the scale where crews search, together with a developing framework for their regional consequences. The final delivery workshop, rights-holder and operator co-interpretation, and transparent data releases will determine how those capabilities become useful routine practice.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-hmsc
#| tbl-cap: "HMSC production fits: training rows, convergence diagnostics and apparent (in-sample) AUC for the mapped cull target, and the share of mapped 120 m cells each component fills. All passed the gates (minimum effective sample size ≥ 400, maximum upper PSRF ≤ 1.1)."

  Component = hsum$component,
  `Training rows` = int(hsum$rows),
  `Min ESS` = int(hsum$min_ess),
  `Max upper PSRF` = a3(hsum$max_psrf_upper),
  `Apparent AUC` = a3(hsum$apparent_auc),
  `Share of mapped cells` = vapply(hsum$component, function(x) p1(pick(hcov, component = x, col = "fraction")), ""),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrrr")
```
